title: Andy Burnham to push for new post-Brexit deals at EU summit
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told MPs he will push for new post-Brexit deals with the EU at a summit next month.He said "deeper cooperation" on som
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told MPs he will push for new post-Brexit deals with the EU at a summit next month.He said "deeper cooperation" on some key issues - including youth mobility, food and drink, and energy - would help drive economic growth in the UK.In a statement to MPs, Burnham also warned the EU's Made In Europe plans posed "a risk to UK manufacturing" and said he was in talks to get "an arrangement" that worked for the UK. The EU proposals aim to protect EU industry from Chinese competitors but could impact British industry and supply chains.But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the prime minister was "unpicking" the deal the UK signed with the EU.Although he said he was keen to negotiate a closer relationship with the EU, Burnham made clear Labour's manifesto commitments not to return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement, would stay in place until the next election.Burnham said the "immediate priority" was securing a successful outcome at the November summit, adding: "I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term."At every stage, the British public will be the boss, and I am clear that public opinion currently supports a pragmatic approach like the one I am suggesting."While the prime minister has committed to the current Labour manifesto's red lines about Brexit, in interviews after Labour conference, he did not rule out a new manifesto, which could include re-joining the EU.It is increasingly clear that economic growth, and cooperation on illegal immigration, are going to be at the centre of No 10's arguments when it comes to selling a closer relationship both at - and beyond - next month's summit.The Brexit withdrawal agreement in 2020 agreed the UK's "divorce bill" payments to the EU, and allowed the rules and regulations in the UK to start to diverge from those in the EU, which was necessary in order to negotiate trade deal with other countries.But the divergence in food standards caused problems for UK food exports to its largest market, a problem that Sir Keir Starmer started to try to fix by renegotiating some common rules to reduce red tape.In May 2025, this resulted in a post-Brexit deal agreeing continued access to UK waters for EU fishing boats until 2038, in return for a deal to reduce checks on food exports to the EU, which meant the UK was able to sell raw burgers and sausages back into the EU for the first time since Brexit.The summit next month will see a series of deals with the EU on the table, Burnham told MPs, including food and drink, energy trading, and coordinating on immigration.Burnham claimed these agreements could add the equivalent of £10bn per year to the economy by 2040, arguing that it would be a "dereliction of duty" to turn away from the chance to cut bureaucracy."At present entire truckloads of plants or fresh produce can be destroyed because of a single missing stamp or a minor paperwork delay," he said."Fresh meat and fish spoil while waiting in trucks, and tonnes of exports have to be written off. Our largest food export, Scottish salmon, faces a 100% rate of document checks at the border, costing us around £100m in lost exports."British burgers and other fresh meat products cannot be sold in the EU, seed potatoes from Scotland and shellfish from Wales are banned - this is having a real impact on businesses and the agreement on the table could reverse some of that damage."The prime minister said a fresh agreement at the EU summit would also "ease the pressure on prices in the supermarket".He said securing an energy deal, involving emissions trading, could "lower energy costs for households and businesses alike", adding this could cut wholesale energy costs by 20% in Northern Ireland.Burnham said he also hoped to rebuild links with EU police and security agencies to boost information-sharing and help tackle smuggling gangs.And he said being open about a new relationship with the EU was necessary to get a good deal on all these things: "If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation we must have."Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain."The Conservative leader criticised the prime minister for "unpicking the deal this country signed with the EU a decade after the referendum".Badenoch added Burnham would not get a better deal than the one secured by the Conservatives, accusing him of giving the game away ahead of the summit."His exact words earlier this year were, 'the last thing we should do right now is re-run those arguments' and yet here he is unpicking the deal this country signed with the EU a decade after the referendum," she said."He is not going to get a better deal. The EU are tough negotiators, and it's not just that the EU are tough negotiators, he has already revealed his entire negotiating hand."He has just blurted out everything he wants in this statement and I will tell him now, as a former trade secretary, this is not how you conduct negotiations."Mocking the previous negotiations, Burnham said: "She says that, oh, I've revealed what I want to do and this isn't any way to negotiate it - because the Tories were so good, weren't they, at negotiating deals with our partners?"Conservative Nigel Huddleston pointed out that post-Brexit trade deals with countries like the US and India meant a new EU deal would not be straightforward.He said: "As a former trade minister can I also advise the PM, because his officials and minsters clearly have not, that actually it may not be as easy after all, because of clauses in some of the 70-something other trade deals that we did with other countries, to unwind all the things he would like to do."However, Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey welcomed Burnham's recognition of  the "damage" of Brexit and called on him to go further, dropping Labour's red lines and opening negotiations on joining the EU single market and customs union.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham to push for new post-Brexit deals at EU summit

title: Breaking Bad actor RJ Mitte dies aged 34
description: US actor RJ Mitte, best known for his role as the defiant son of drug kingpin Walter White in the drama series Breaking Bad, has died aged 34."It is w
body: US actor RJ Mitte, best known for his role as the defiant son of drug kingpin Walter White in the drama series Breaking Bad, has died aged 34."It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte," his representative told the BBC.He died in Brownsville, Texas. No immediate cause of death was provided. Mitte, who lived with cerebral palsy, drew on his own experience for his role as Walter White Jr in the Emmy-winning drama series starring Bryan Cranston and Aaron Paul. He earned a Screen Actors Guild Award in 2014 for his work on the series."Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion," his representative, Sean Reilly, said in a statement to the BBC. Mitte also served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children's. He created The Mitte Foundation as well, to support philanthropic efforts and community initiatives, using his platform "to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation for people with disabilities", Reilly said.The Brownsville Police Department confirmed the actor's passing in a statement to the BBC, saying the cause and manner of death have not been determined and the investigation remains ongoing. No foul play was suspected, according to police.The actor was declared dead on 12 October at what was believed to be his home, Cameron County Justice of the Peace, Cyndi Hinojosa, told the Associated Press, adding that a post-mortem examination would be performed. Breaking Bad aired on US cable broadcaster AMC for five seasons from 2008-13. The anti-hero drama created by Vince Gilligan earned a whopping 58 Primetime Emmy nominations and won 16, including two for Outstanding Drama Series in 2013 and 2014. Cranston plays a high school chemistry teacher in New Mexico who turns to a life of crime to support his family after a cancer diagnosis. As he descends deeper into the underbelly of the meth trade, he drifts further from his son, Walt Jr, who makes his displeasure known with levity through much of the series.The actor posted a tribute to his on-screen son on Instagram, writing that he was in "deep despair" following news of Mitte's death. "I met him when he was only 14 years old when he was cast as Walter White Jr., a part he played with such joy and enthusiasm," said Cranston."That kid was pretty raw when we started shooting the pilot in February of 2007, but little by little we watched him grow into a really fine actor."Cranston wrote of Mitte's advocacy for performers with disabilities, and noted that he never allowed his cerebral palsy to "be an excuse for anything"."All that promise and potential now is such a loss," wrote the actor, adding that he "thoroughly enjoyed being with him throughout the years on the series, and after the spotlight on Breaking Bad dimmed". "I'll miss you, son," he said.In a statement shared with the Hollywood Reporter, Aaron Paul, who played one of the show's lead characters, Jesse Pinkman, said he was at a loss and heartbroken."RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed," he said. "And to whoever happens to be reading this, please know you are loved, and you are not alone. Always remember that." Dean Norris, who played Mitte's uncle, Hank Schrader, posted that although "RJ didn't play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set". "He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed," Norris wrote.Mitte, who grew up in Louisiana, was a young teen when he auditioned for the breakthrough role after moving to Los Angeles to support his younger sister's acting career in 2005.He had said that his first audition in Los Angeles was for a California state public service announcement for an anti-meth commercial. "Fast forward to auditioning for Breaking Bad, which is still, in my opinion, an anti-meth thing because it doesn't end well for anyone," he said on the Joe Vulpis Podcast earlier this month.His character was based on Gilligan's late friend who had a more severe case of cerebral palsy and used forearm crutches, which Mitte did not require. Mitte was seen as playing the role with honesty and accessibility, cracking jokes as a teen whose health condition was never mentioned in the series.After shooting to fame, Mitte fought for more varied roles and complex depictions of characters with disabilities, both visible and invisible."Whenever awards season rolls around, we always hope to see a diverse group of projects that reflect all of us, in body and mind," he told the BBC in 2021. "Watching the awareness grow around disability representation has been great to see, but breakthroughs sometimes come in pieces and moments instead of larger change," he said.Mitte's other on-screen credits include Hannah Montana, Switched at Birth, Westhampton and his latest project, Talking to Strangers, which came out earlier this year. Additional reporting by Rebecka Pieder

schema.headline: Breaking Bad actor RJ Mitte dies aged 34

title: Which war is having the biggest impact on diesel prices - Iran or Ukraine?
description: ByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondent, BBC VerifyUS President Donald Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for the global
body: ByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondent, BBC VerifyUS President Donald Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for the global reduction in diesel exports and the spike in prices around the world, saying President Volodymyr Zelensky "wants to make problems for the world"."He'd better damn well stop," Trump said, before suggesting Ukraine should "get a new leader who can make a deal".But others have pointed the finger of blame at the US-Israel war with Iran for cutting exports of the refined fuel from the Gulf region.After Trump announced a controversial deal to import diesel from Russia - promising "lower prices for Americans" - BBC Verify has looked at what has been affecting supplies of the fuel in recent months and years.The figures suggest that while both the Ukraine and Iran conflicts have significantly reduced global diesel exports - the fall in supplies from the Gulf states due to the war with Iran has been greater.What's happened to global diesel prices?While the rising cost of diesel directly hits drivers, there's a wider concern because of its use in the lorries, vans and ships that form the backbone of global supply chains. Any increase in transport costs could be fed through to consumers in the form of higher prices.Average US retail diesel prices on 5 October were $6.20 (£4.69) per gallon, just shy of the record of $6.50 per gallon seen on 21 September, according to the latest figures from the US Energy Information Administration.Before the war with Iran a gallon of diesel in the US cost around $3.50.Similarly, average UK diesel prices are currently touching record highs, with data from the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero showing that on 5 October a litre cost 199p.In 2025, around 6.8 million barrels of diesel per day were being exported to the global market, according to figures from the shipping data company Kpler. Exports account for around a quarter of total global diesel consumption. The rest comes from countries' domestic production.In September 2026, global exports had fallen to 5.8 million barrels per day - a decline of around one million barrels per day.Some countries, notably the US, have increased their diesel exports over the past year, but overall net global exports have declined.And analysts say it's that drop which has been responsible for pushing up the retail price of diesel.How much supply has been lost from Russia?In 2025 Russia was exporting around 810,000 barrels of diesel per day but by September 2026 that had fallen to around 140,000 barrels per day - a decline of around 670,000 barrels per day.Jonathan Leader Maynard, from King's College London, says "many analysts" would see the decline in Russia's exports of oil products, including diesel, as being "primarily due to Ukraine's drone attacks" rather than international sanctions.How much supply has been lost from the Middle East?As well as being a major exporter of crude oil, the Middle East is also a significant global hub for the production of diesel.In 2025 the Gulf states - Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman - were exporting around 1.4 million barrels of diesel per day.In September 2026 that had fallen to around 670,000 barrels per day.This sharp decline has been driven by the impact of the US-Iran war on the flow of exports of refined diesel from the Gulf states through the Strait of Hormuz. Traffic flows in the waterway have been badly disrupted by Iranian strikes on tankers and the US blockade of Iran's ports.While estimates from ship-tracking firms suggest the flow of crude oil through the waterway returned close to pre-war levels last month - due, in part, to the US navy helping to protect shipping - the flow of refined diesel from the Middle East has remained far below pre-war levels.So which conflict is more to blame?The figures suggest the conflict with Iran has had a greater impact on the global drop in diesel export volumes than the Ukraine war.Exports from Russia are down around 670,000 barrels a day compared with a fall of around 810,000 from the Middle EastThough analysts stress both are significant."The US-Iran conflict delivered a major shock to global energy markets in 2026, but the ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict is now amplifying this pressure by taking Russian refineries offline," Paul de Leeuw, director of the Energy Transition Institute at Robert Gordon University, told BBC Verify.His comments were echoed by Rory Johnson, an oil analyst at Commodity Context, who said Ukraine's attacks are "bringing the pain of the war to the Russian homeland and largely knocking the world's second-largest diesel exporter out of the market".Additional reporting by Nicholas Barrett and Joshua CheethamCharts by Erwan Rivault

schema.headline: Which war is having the biggest impact on diesel prices - Iran or Ukraine?

title: One dead, several others hurt on Six Flags rollercoaster in Georgia
description: Officials have not said how the person was killed. The BBC has contacted local police and fire authorities, as well as park officials.Witnesses told l
body: Officials have not said how the person was killed. The BBC has contacted local police and fire authorities, as well as park officials.Witnesses told local media they saw a man ejected from the ride, accounts that the BBC has not verified.Local outlet 11Alive quoted, external a witness saying the man fell from the rollercoaster on to the roof of a haunted house attraction.A park spokesperson said in a statement that its team and local authorities had responded immediately, and they were co-operating on an investigation into the incident.Mableton Mayor Michael Owens said the city's public safety director was co-ordinating with local police and park security on the situation.The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five.Monday's death is the latest of several at the Georgia amusement park, according to personal injury attorneys. The fatalities include a 45-year-old man dying from an apparent heart attack after riding the Goliath in 2006, said the Doan Law Firm.Six Flags is the largest amusement park operator in North America, with 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico.The incident comes just weeks after one of its parks in southern California announced it would close the popular X2 roller coaster after more than 100 people alleged brain injuries from the ride.Six Flags said the ride had passed a range of safety tests, but that it had decided to retire it because it was "the right thing to do".

schema.headline: One dead, several others hurt on Six Flags rollercoaster in Georgia

title: Heating oil customers face tough winter despite shake-up promise
description: Heating oil customers facing soaring bills have been promised better regulation of the sector by the government.Ministers say they will tighten up rul
body: Heating oil customers facing soaring bills have been promised better regulation of the sector by the government.Ministers say they will tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things go wrong. Minimum order levels, set for some customers, will be reviewed.With prices close to having doubled in the past year, some campaigners have called for heating oil customers to benefit from the same cap as regular, variable gas and electricity tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales.But there is no sign of the government proposing such a change, nor when the stricter rules will take effect.Ministers said they would work with industry to "develop a regulatory regime for the heating oil market, protecting consumers and promoting competition".In the meantime, oil users have been offered discounts on heat pumps, a code of practice is in place, and industry practices setting minimum order volumes at 500 litres for some consumers will be reviewed. Domestic tanks typically hold between 1,000 and 2,000 litres.The government said this had left some people having to pay for more heating oil than they might need.Nick, a heating oil customer from West Suffolk, told the BBC's Your Voice that "off-grid households remain a major policy blind spot" for the government."Any protection from UK government for domestic heating oil users will be very welcome, providing this is for all domestic heating oil users," the 28-year-old said.He rents a three-bedroom home with his partner. He said they had seen prices more than double in a year, to quotes of 111p per litre."Heating my home is now no longer another household bill, but almost an investment," he said.He called on tax cuts for customers, or the extension of the price cap to heating oil - a demand also made by charity National Energy Action.Tim Buckman, chief executive of price comparison site Boiler Juice, told the BBC he wants stronger protections for consumers but the main problem was that heating oil is twice as expensive as it was before the war. "Just putting regulation in place is not going to reduce the price for customers. What we would like to see is the VAT off heating oil or targeting that specifically."Some 1.5 million households depend on heating oil, but they do not have the same consumer protections as electricity and gas customers.However, energy regulator Ofgem, which sets the cap for standard variable tariffs, only covers England, Wales and Scotland.Most heating oil customers are in Northern Ireland, where 60% of households rely on it, but where regulation is separate.It is likely Ofgem will regulate heating oil in England, Scotland and Wales, and the UK government said it would "engage with the Northern Ireland Executive as they consider these recommendations in parallel".

schema.headline: Heating oil customers face tough winter despite shake-up promise

title: Miliband says Britain won't tolerate threats on our soil, as Iran ambassador summoned
description: The foreign secretary has summoned the Iranian ambassador to make clear that "Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil" following last month's in
body: The foreign secretary has summoned the Iranian ambassador to make clear that "Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil" following last month's incident at RAF Fairford.Ed Miliband said attempts by Iran to undermine the UK's security "through its criminal networks, proxy groups and state-backed malign activity is unacceptable".Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs the incident in Gloucestershire was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard", while the home secretary said the likely coordinator was a "known individual based in Iran".Iran's ambassador to the UK, Seyed Ali Mousavi, said Tehran was not involved and was willing to cooperate with British authorities.The Foreign Office has also sanctioned two Iranians, including the head of the regime's counterespionage operations - with both men subjected to travel bans and asset freezes.Burnham also indicated Iran could be hit with further sanctions over its suspected role.It comes as the UK and 28 other countries - including the US, Canada, Australia, France and Germany - issued a joint statement condemning "in the strongest terms" violent attacks by Iran. The statement accuses Tehran of carrying out "lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities" and also recognises the UK's attribution of Iranian involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.A huge police operation began after officers were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the base in the early hours of 27 September.Dozens of homes were evacuated in the nearby village of Whelford and a large cordon was put in place around the site.So far, a total of seven men - all in their 20s - have been arrested and later bailed in connection with the incident. No one has been charged.Last week, Downing Street insisted the airbase was safe after the US withdrew all of its bombers – about a dozen B-1s from the base – back to their home stations on American soil.In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".RAF Fairford, in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades.In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved an American request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.A US state department spokesman confirmed that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had a call with Miliband on Monday where they discussed "holding Iran to account for its actions and of continued collaboration to secure US assets in the United Kingdom".

schema.headline: Miliband says Britain won't tolerate threats on our soil, as Iran ambassador summoned

title: UK growth upgraded but energy prices and rates to bite in 2027
description: The UK economy is forecast to grow by more than previously expected this year before higher energy prices and interest rates hit growth in 2027, the I
body: The UK economy is forecast to grow by more than previously expected this year before higher energy prices and interest rates hit growth in 2027, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has said.The organisation's latest report, which is closely watched by the government, said the UK economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027.Economies across the world have proved more resilient to the energy price shock caused by the US-Iran war, the IMF said, but it warned the economic fallout from the conflict remained "highly uncertain".Chancellor John Healey said the government would look to "provide some breathing space" for households in the Budget.Healey is making the final preparations to Andy Burnham's new-look government's tax and spending plans, which will be announced on 28 October. Government borrowing costs have surged, placing pressure on the chancellor to ensure his plans are credible in the eyes of financial markets, which the UK relies on to borrow money.But IMF Chief Economist Silvana Tenreyro told BBC News on Tuesday that the UK's process of managing its debts is now leading the major G7 economies."As you know, the UK has already started the consolidation process and it is the country that basically stands out, along with India", she said at the launch of the IMF's new global forecast, the World Economic Outlook.The organisation said the UK is one of the only major economies on course to stabilise levels of national debt. It projects the UK will reduce its annual borrowing by nearly four percentage points of GDP from 2025 to 2031, significantly more than the rest of the G7, many of which are increasing their deficit over this time period.The UK is also projected to have the lowest annual borrowing in the G7 in 2031, and the longest maturity of debt, locking in lower rates for longer.Asked if the UK was one of the countries the IMF was telling to reduce borrowing, Tenreyro said that the country had begun the process already and should "stay the course".The head of the IMF has previously called on the world's advanced economies to cut borrowing and reduce debt levels.The reversal of downgrades to economic forecasts made at the start of the US-Iran war, mean the UK is expected to have the second-fasted growing economy in the G7 along with Germany.But growth is estimated to slow in 2027 to 1.2% due to higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weighing on household spending and business investment.Healey acknowledged that wars in the Middle East and Europe were "hitting people in the UK and around the world", but added that "Britain's economy is showing strong international resilience".When the economy is growing, businesses tend to invest more, more jobs are created and people, on average, tend to feel better off. The opposite can occur if the economy stagnates or shrinks.Economists have suggested Healey faces having to find £35bn to avoid cuts to public spending while meeting defence promises in his first Budget.On Tuesday, the Resolution Foundation called on the chancellor to make "make repairs" to the public finances, but said well-targeted support was needed for those "struggling to heat their homes"."The challenge of continuing to bring down borrowing must be paired with the pressing need for fresh cost of living support to help families facing a difficult winter ahead," the think tank said.Andrew Griffith, Conservative shadow chancellor, said if Healey "reaches for more tax rises" in his Budget, "he is choosing slower growth and working people will pay for it".Burnham has pledged to create "good growth in every postcode" as part of his plans to giving nations and regions more control, but his strategy has faced criticism inside his own party.The IMF said households are likely to continue feeling the pinch of rising prices, with inflation expected to average 3.3% this year and remain above the Bank of England's 2% target in 2027 at 2.8%.The Bank itself has predicted inflation could rise above 4% at the beginning of next year - making it more likely that interest rates will rise.Healey is expected to meet with other finance ministers at the IMF's annual meeting in Bangkok, Thailand, on Tuesday to discuss how the economic impact of the Middle East and European conflicts could be limited.The IMF said the global economy had shown a "remarkable capacity to absorb shocks" not just from the current Middle East conflict, but also from the Covid pandemic and Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

schema.headline: UK growth upgraded but energy prices and rates to bite in 2027

title: US actress Selma Blair accused of assault after incident with flight attendants
description: US actress Selma Blair has been issued with a summons accusing her of assault after she allegedly attacked attendants on a plane, officials say. The L
body: US actress Selma Blair has been issued with a summons accusing her of assault after she allegedly attacked attendants on a plane, officials say. The Legally Blonde star was investigated by the FBI following an alleged altercation on a Delta Air Lines flight from Los Angeles to New York.Airport officials said they had responded to a call on Sunday about "a physically abusive passenger" on the flight. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said.Blair, 54, who also starred in Hellboy and Cruel Intentions, was arrested and taken to hospital. Her publicist told the BBC she had "experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct"."Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition," her publicist said.On Monday, a federal law enforcement source told the BBC that Blair had been issued a summons for a charge of assault within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the US. The source said she will be required to appear at the petty violation court in Brooklyn, New York City, but no date has been set. The incident occurred around 23:00 local time aboard Delta Airlines Flight 938.According to the BBC's US media partner, CBS News, the flight crew allegedly restrained Blair on the plane. Air traffic control audio obtained by CBS included the pilot calling for medical personnel to come to the plane, citing a "bloody nose as well as some bite marks".A spokesperson for Delta said law enforcement responded as the flight arrived at John F Kennedy International Airport in New York, and that there was no operational impact to the flight because of the incident."Delta has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first," Delta Air Lines said in a statement to the BBC. Blair largely retreated from film work after her 2018 multiple sclerosis (MS) diagnosis, telling the BBC years later that she blamed the disease for taking "my career down" because "I had to stop working". Before the incident on Sunday, Blair posted on Instragram about her extensive travels with her service dog Scout, an English Red Fox Labrador she got in 2021 to help with her neurological condition."From LA to New Mexico to La to nyc to LA Scout and I have been busy. I miss you," she wrote alongside a video that included footage of a city taken from a plane window. In 2021, she announced she was in remission for the disease.In 2016, she had another incident on a flight after a drunken outburst caused two nurses to have to subdue her on board. Blair issued a public apology after the incident. She said she accidentally mixed her medication with alcohol and "made a big mistake" that caused her to "black out" and "say and do things that I deeply regret"."I am a flawed human being who makes mistakes and am filled with shame over this incident. I am truly very sorry," she said at the time.US media reported in that instance that the actress was screaming uncontrollably and nurses had to prop her up with a pillow and give her oxygen to calm down.She was taken off the plane on a stretcher when the flight landed in Los Angeles from Mexico, and was taken to hospital.In her 2022 memoir Mean Baby, Blair wrote about biting celebrities Sienna Miller, Seth MacFarlane and Kate Moss.She wrote that she bit people when "my system gets overwhelmed and instantaneously short-circuits".

schema.headline: US actress Selma Blair accused of assault after incident with flight attendants

title: Bumble shares soar after report dating firm in $1bn takeover talks
description: Shares in dating app company Bumble soared by almost 50% on Monday after a report that it is in advanced talks to be bought for around $1bn (£757m).Te
body: Shares in dating app company Bumble soared by almost 50% on Monday after a report that it is in advanced talks to be bought for around $1bn (£757m).Technology holding company Ithaca could announce a deal to buy the Texas-based firm as early as this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.The jump in Bumble's shares pushed its stock market valuation to over $580m but that is still far below a peak of more than $14bn it reached after listing on the Nasdaq in 2021.Bumble is one of the world's most downloaded dating apps, operating in a crowded market where growth has slowed. The BBC has contacted Bumble and Ithaca for comment.Bumble was launched in 2014 by Whitney Wolfe Herd, who was also a co-founder of dating app giant Tinder.Wolfe Herd built Bumble's brand around a distinctive feature that only allowed women to initiate conversations with matches.It recently abandoned that rule, prompting debate among users over whether the app had lost what set it apart from rivals."Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides," Wolfe Herd said in August.Dating apps like Bumble have come under pressure in recent years as some younger users have grown disillusioned with browsing for dates.Bumble said in 2025 that it would cut almost a third of its workforce as the industry grappled with what Wolfe Herd described as an "inflection point" in online dating.Investments in other dating companies have also soured as apps have struggled to convince users to pay for their services.Match Group - which owns apps including Tinder, OkCupid and Hinge - has also seen its shares fall sharply from their peak in 2021.According a report by media watchdog Ofcom in 2025, adults in the UK were spending less time on dating apps compared to three years earlier.Some single people are instead turning to board game get-togethers, book clubs and other group activities in the hope of finding a partner.

schema.headline: Bumble shares soar after report dating firm in $1bn takeover talks

title: Government expands police support to political figures who are not MPs
description: Political figures who are not currently MPs will be given police support, the home secretary has announced.Shabana Mahmood told MPs there was "insuffi
body: Political figures who are not currently MPs will be given police support, the home secretary has announced.Shabana Mahmood told MPs there was "insufficient protection" for those serving in public life and that the new announcement will cover peers, former MPs and party spokespeople.She also announced an urgent, independent review of security arrangements for high-profile figures including politicians and royals. It comes three months after Reform UK spokeswoman and former Conservative MP Ann Widdecombe was found dead at her home in Devon, having been hit on the head with a hammer 21 times as she ate lunch.Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with her murder, and he was also charged with preparing acts of terror against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.Kerry is alleged to have carried out research on prominent targets over a period of two years, including trying to gain entry into Farage's London home.Speaking in the Commons on Monday, Mahmood said that "robust debate and criticism are part of this job - threats, abuse and violence are not."She did not elaborate on what the support would involve, but told MPs it would include access to a named police officer and help with wider security measures.The safety of politicians has been a prominent issue in recent years, following the murders of Conservative MP Sir David Amess in 2021 and Labour MP Jo Cox in 2016."We owe it to them and to everyone who believes in a fair and open country to ensure that those who serve at all levels receive the protection they deserve," Mahmood added.The "root and branch" independent review into security arrangements will be led by former national security advisor Stephen Lovegrove, and will look into "physical threats, online risks and the dangers posed within our more polarised society".Mahmood confirmed that the review will report within six months, and build on the existing work of Sir Robert Buckland, who is leading a separate review into the murder of Sir David.In response, shadow home secretary Chris Philp welcomed the extension of protective measures, saying threats to elected representatives are threats to democracy.Reform UK's home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf welcomed the review, but added: "It is disappointing that it took the murder of one of our colleagues, countless threats towards our party spokespeople and months of campaigning from Reform UK to make this government take action."Reform has in recent months accused the government of a "dereliction of duty" over Farage's taxpayer-funded security, claiming it had previously been "downgraded" - a charge that the Home Office has said is "categorically untrue".Decisions over the security of current MPs and members of the House of Lords are made by the House of Parliament's security team.There is a separate, independent committee, the Royal and VIP Executive Committee (Ravec), to deal with high-profile political candidates, which is staffed by officials from the Home Office, the Cabinet Office, and the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.The Jo Cox Foundation welcomed the home secretary's announcement but said "strengthening physical security" alone was not enough."We must also tackle the root causes - including online harms and education - to prevent future attacks," its chief executive Olivia Field said in a statement on X.According to data released to the BBC in April, the number of alleged offences against MPs have increased year-on-year, with 976 recorded in 2025, compared to 364 in 2019.MPs reported 4,064 crimes to the Met's Parliamentary Liaison Team between 2019 and 2025. Most offences were related to malicious communications followed by harassment, and criminal damage to a building.In 2025, there were 50 death threats reported - up from 31 the previous year.

schema.headline: Government expands police support to political figures who are not MPs

title: Abramovich’s close associate misled UK court in £1bn oil-fields case, documents suggest
description: One of Roman Abramovich's closest associates misled a UK court to help secure ownership of Siberian oil fields, leaked documents seen by the BBC sugge
body: One of Roman Abramovich's closest associates misled a UK court to help secure ownership of Siberian oil fields, leaked documents seen by the BBC suggest.Eugene Tenenbaum, a former director of Chelsea Football Club, helped to manage the billionaire's wealth at the time of the case in 2008, which Abramovich won.Tenenbaum was giving evidence during proceedings taken against Abramovich by a company owned by another Russian billionaire, who was claiming the oil fields had been stolen from him and other investors.The leaked documents now suggest there was a premeditated attempt by Abramovich to reduce the value of the other investors' stake in the Siberian venture.Roman Abramovich's lawyers say their "client denies all the allegations made against him".Lawyers for Eugene Tenenbaum say he "denies in the strongest terms any suggestion that he committed perjury or contempt of court".The 2008 court case centred on the ownership of Siberian oil fields being developed jointly between Abramovich's company, Sibneft, and the Russian subsidiary of the British company, Sibir Energy PLC, owned by Russian billionaire Chalva Tchigirinsky.Sibneft contributed money, while the subsidiary Yugraneft provided the licences for the oil fields.Their partnership - which became known as Sibneft-Yugra - ended acrimoniously. Sibir's 50% interest in the joint venture had been diluted, or reduced, to less than 1%. It said this had been done without its knowledge.Unsuccessful attempts to sue Sibneft in both Russia and the British Virgin Islands led to the court proceedings in London.At court in 2008, Yugraneft claimed "to have been the victim of a massive fraud directed by Mr Abramovich", as a result of which it had suffered a loss of "not less that $2 billion", which in 2008 was worth about £1bn.But Abramovich's team claimed that Yugraneft had been unable to repay loans of more than $30m, so lost its right over the shares.Abramovich won the case on a number of fronts, including that Yugraneft's case had been an abuse of process.However, Panorama has uncovered new evidence suggesting the court was misled, in a joint investigation with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, external.The evidence is contained in a leak of documents about Abramovich's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus between 1995 and 2022. It raises serious questions about the integrity of some of the oligarch's professional advisers.We have already found that the world's biggest accountancy firm, Deloitte, helped in falsifying documents to hide his wealth and evade tax.The BBC and media partners including the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project and the Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network - as well the Bureau of Investigative Journalism - have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential investigation, external.In the High Court, lawyers for Yugraneft argued the case should be heard in London, and that Tenenbaum, who was based there at the time, must have been aware of the dilution of Yugraneft's interest.But Tenenbaum denied this and told the court "he only became aware of Sibneft-Yugra in Spring 2004".He also testified he had "searched" his "files, emails and documents from 2002 to 2004" and had in his "possession no records or documents or other communications that relate to Sibneft-Yugra".But the leaked documents suggest he misled the court.They show that in October 2003, months before Tenenbaum said he first became aware of Sibneft-Yugra, he had authorised Abramovich's purchase of shares in the joint venture.Two months later, Tenenbaum authorised another financial deal related to Sibneft-Yugra.Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, told Panorama that it would be "very serious" if Tenenbaum's 2008 evidence was false and that it could "range from being perjury, to an attempt to pervert the course of justice, to being a contempt of the court".Tenenbaum's lawyers told us "he gave his evidence honestly and in good faith" and that he "cannot recall the context or detail of documents" more than 20 years old.The judge made clear in his 2008 judgement that Tenenbaum's knowledge of the Sibneft-Yugra deal would not have made a difference to his decision, however the leak also suggests some of the documents presented by Abramovich's legal team to the High Court had been falsified.One of the agreements was dated August 2003, but appears not to have been created or actually signed until 2007.Abramovich's team had argued in court that Yugraneft's interest had been diluted because of the need for finance for the joint venture.They claimed Tchigirinsky had approached them "in the spring of 2002" with a view to new financing arrangements. Tchigirinsky denied this was the case.The leaked documents show that before then, in January 2002, Abramovich's Russian associates had already prepared a bundle of documents.They included agreements under which two Abramovich companies would acquire shares in Sibneft-Yugra, increasing his stake and diluting Yugraneft's.This evidence suggests they were already planning to dilute Yugraneft's interest and that the argument they used in court about financing was a smokescreen.Lawyers for Abramovich said: "The Judgment made no finding that the dilution was premeditated", or that it was "fraudulent". They added: "The Judge found that our client received no property belonging to Yugraneft, and that no Yugraneft asset could be traced into his hands."

schema.headline: Abramovich’s close associate misled UK court in £1bn oil-fields case, documents suggest

title: Michael Jordan jersey from 'Last Dance' season sells for record £10.6m
description: A Michael Jordan jersey from his 'Last Dance' season has sold for $14m (£10.6m), a record for a piece of basketball memorabilia.Jordan wore the Chicag
body: A Michael Jordan jersey from his 'Last Dance' season has sold for $14m (£10.6m), a record for a piece of basketball memorabilia.Jordan wore the Chicago Bulls jersey during game two of the 1998 NBA Finals and has autographed it too.He scored a game-high 37 points that evening before ending his last season with the Bulls with a 4-2 series win for his sixth and final NBA Championship. He was named the Finals' Most Valuable Player in all six.The only item of sports memorabilia that has cost more is the jersey worn by baseball legend Babe Ruth when he "called the shot" during the 1932 World Series, which was sold for $24.1m (£18.2m) in 2024.The previous high for a basketball item was a card featuring Jordan and Kobe Bryant from 2007-08 which sold for $12.9m (£9.8m) last year.The previous record for a piece of game-worn Jordan memorabilia was set just two weeks ago when his jersey from game three of the 1998 Finals, which is not autographed, sold via auction for $12.3m (£9.3m).The latest purchase was made by Miami real estate investor Ron Firman in a private sale through Hunt Auctions.David Hunt, president of Hunt Auctions, said in a statement: "While Michael Jordan's importance within the sports memorabilia marketplace has long been established, it has now escalated to an elite asset class more typically reserved for iconic works of art."

schema.headline: Michael Jordan jersey from 'Last Dance' season sells for record £10.6m

title: 'I lost my hair to MS - now now my wigs are worn by Serena Williams and Naomi Campbell
description: Image source, Antonia Okonma ShittuImage caption, Antonia with model Naomi Campbell, who is one of her clientsByElla KiplingWhen Antonia Okonma Shittu
body: Image source, Antonia Okonma ShittuImage caption, Antonia with model Naomi Campbell, who is one of her clientsByElla KiplingWhen Antonia Okonma Shittu was told she had multiple sclerosis (MS) and would be using a wheelchair within the year, she was in denial. The 26-year-old, who was in between acting jobs and working in a call centre, said the diagnosis was a "massive turning point" in her life. "It does really make you think about what you want to do in life," she said. She looked back to what she enjoyed doing as a child - styling hair - and decided to use the shock of the diagnosis to spur her on to turn her passion into a business.Antonia, who grew up on a council estate in west London, bought two wigs and went door to door selling them from the boot of her car.Image source, Antonia Okonma ShittuImage caption, Antonia with American actress Niecey NashAlmost two decades later, she is now a multi-million-pound brand owner, with high-profile clients including tennis icon Serena Williams, model Naomi Campbell and actress Niecey Nash. She even won a Black British Business Award last week.Antonia, now 44, still struggles with her health, having also received diagnoses of Graves' disease - an autoimmune condition - and heart failure, but hopes her experience running a hair empire while fitting in hospital appointments can inspire other women.'I didn't feel like myself after losing my hair'Antonia says she saw a gap in the market when she was surrounded by "terrible" wigs while working in TV and film, including in the ITV series Bad Girls two decades ago."Women wanted natural-looking wigs and they just weren't available. They looked like helmets!"Antonia set up a Facebook page and began advertising on Gumtree. "I had very limited resources. I didn't have any investors behind me. I come from very humble beginnings."Her experience dealing with MS has helped her success, she says. Antonia lost her hair when she underwent chemotherapy following a bone marrow transplant, so she knows what it is like to be "completely bald".This made her relate more deeply to her customers, she explains, as she understands the loss of control some women feel when they lose their hair."I didn't feel like myself," she says, "but being able to put on a wig that looks something close to how your hair was, or the look you used to have, it's as though you can feel like yourself again."When she sees a woman put a wig on and her "whole face lights up", it can be "very, very rewarding"."When we feel good about ourselves...we're more confident, we can achieve more. I felt like I was changing the world, one person at a time."Image source, Antonia Okonma ShittuImage caption, Antonia experienced hair loss after undergoing chemotherapyBalancing health and businessWhile Antonia's business, A-List Lace Hair, has grown from strength to strength, with salons in London and New York, she has been dealing with the impact of her health conditions.She struggles with fatigue due to her MS and uses a wheelchair, but says this has not stopped her success. Instead, it has simply changed the way she has run her business."I used to feel that being a good entrepreneur was being able to do as much as I can myself," Antonia said. "Due to my health challenges, there are days where I literally can't feel my legs, they feel like jelly, there's days where I'm completely exhausted after sleeping, I wake up completely shattered." This has forced her to "trust other people and gain strength in building a team".Image source, 365 style concierge & Karanjee GabaImage caption, Antonia says she wants to remain open about her health to inspire other women in businessAs a woman in business, being in a wheelchair can sometimes make Antonia feel "smaller" as people often have to look down at her at industry events. "People are often surprised when I start speaking about my business, as though they're thinking 'how have you accomplished all of this in a wheelchair?'"Antonia, who has three young children, says that being underestimated can be a good thing, and she wants to remain open about her health to inspire other women.She says she used to feel "weak" because of her disability, but now feels she has gained "so much strength" from sharing her experience online.Asked what she would say to another woman who may fear her age, disability or health could get in the way of success, she says: "I would encourage them to just start.""You might not have control over your health, you might not know what tomorrow is going to bring, and you might not have all the resources. But start with what you do have, and let's see what could happen next."

schema.headline: 'I lost my hair to MS - now now my wigs are worn by Serena Williams and Naomi Campbell

title: Afghanistan SAS inquiry: Investigator says team prevented from following evidence
description: A military police investigator has criticised a murder probe into alleged SAS executions, claiming senior officers prevented his team from following t
body: A military police investigator has criticised a murder probe into alleged SAS executions, claiming senior officers prevented his team from following the evidence. Delme Williams, who investigated allegations against one SAS unit, told a public inquiry: "It was not a standard investigation where investigators were making decisions based on where the evidence led them."He added that he remained convinced members of British special forces should have been criminally charged.It is the first time the inquiry, which is examining allegations the SAS committed murders in Afghanistan that were covered up, has heard from those involved in military police investigations into special forces operations.Williams, who served as deputy senior investigative officer for Operation Northmoor which looked at 11 SAS operations, told the inquiry on Monday that the course of the investigation was being "dictated" to his team from above.He added that he questioned whether the senior Royal Military Police officer in charge, known as the Gold commander, was being "influenced to close the investigation".Williams recalled an occasion during Operation Northmoor when investigators were discussing photographs of one of the 11 SAS operations they were investigating for suspected murder.The operation involved the fatal shooting of nine people at a home in Nad Ali district, Helmand Province, in February 2011. The youngest person killed was aged 14.Williams told the inquiry that, based on his experience as a seasoned crime-scene investigator, he wanted to show the images to a forensics expert.Operation Northmoor investigators suspected those shot had been killed unlawfully, and the photographs showed bullet marks low to the ground, which appeared to undermine the SAS account that those killed had been standing and fired at British forces first, before the SAS returned fire.Williams told the public inquiry: "A picture paints a thousand words - photos are ideal evidence."The military police officer said he was "quickly shut down in an abrupt matter" by the Gold commander and when he tried to push back, his senior officer pulled rank and it would have been "insubordinate" to go any further.He said he believed, to this day, the photographs should have examined by an expert.BBC Panorama investigated the same incident and travelled to Helmand to visit the site of the shooting.An RMP investigator confirmed to the BBC that they had seen photographs from the scene and that the bullet mark patterns had raised alarm among the Operation Northmoor team."You can see why we were concerned," the investigator said. "Bullet marks on the walls so low to the ground appeared to undermine the special forces' version of events."Panorama's team examined what appeared to be bullet holes from the raid, still visible, which were clustered together on the walls low to the ground.The BBC showed photographs from the scene to forensics and ballistics experts, who said that the clusters suggested multiple rounds had been fired downward from above, and did not appear indicative of a firefight.This supported the version of events put forward by bereaved family members of some who those were killed. Those relatives have told the BBC those killed were all unarmed civilians who were shot in their beds, and that appears to corroborate the RMP investigators' suspicions.The BBC reported in 2022 evidence from another Operation Northmoor investigator, who told Panorama: "I believe there was pressure from above to shut down the investigation. It became increasingly clear to me that it didn't matter what evidence we were able to gather, these cases were never going to be allowed to go to court."At the time, the Ministry of Defence said the incidents had been subjected to "extensive and independent investigation" by the RMP, and no prosecutions had resulted.Operation Northmoor, set up by the RMP's serious crime team, was investigating 45 killings by an SAS squadron in 2011 during a single tour of Afghanistan.The military police officer told the inquiry the investigation team thought the operational photographs could be important evidence and were looked at "in quite some detail", and the dismissal of this evidence was an example of the way in which the investigation was being run.Williams told the inquiry there were "outside forces" that seemed to him to be directing the course of the investigation. "I do recall a general feeling that inquiries were being stopped too soon and that there was no appetite... to pursue all lines of inquiry or for anyone to be referred for prosecution."During the course of his sworn testimony, Williams was shown a number of internal military documents by the inquiry's lawyers.These records showed it was "confirmed Op NORTHMOOR must end" during an RMP meeting of senior staff in September 2017, while his team were still in the process of gathering evidence.Williams said he was "not surprised" but that criminal investigations "should never be guided by an end date" imposed on them.The military police are supposed to be independent from the wider armed forces, but Williams claimed he was shown a briefing note for a meeting between senior military police officers and the deputy chief of the Army at the end of 2017, which set out the intention to close Northmoor.He remarked he was "surprised to see it written down" but it made sense of the "pressure" he felt the investigation was under.Williams said he still believed individuals should have been referred for prosecution based on the evidence they had found.The inquiry also heard that the former head of the British Army, Sir Nick Carter, asked the RMP to cut the staff working on the murder probe to 25, less than a quarter of the team working on Operation Northmoor in 2016.The police officer in charge at the time, Lt Col John McAllister, believed this would be impossible without having a detrimental effect on the investigation, according to inquiry's lead barrister.Operation Northmoor was the largest ever murder investigation in the Royal Military Police's history but did not result in any charges.Alan Pughsley, expert to the public inquiry, has heavily criticised the lack of resources provided to Operation Northmoor and called the decision to close it "premature and inappropriate".The public inquiry was set up in 2022, following reporting by BBC Panorama that linked one SAS squadron to 54 suspicious deaths on a single six-month tour of Afghanistan.Panorama found evidence suggesting that members of the SAS had executed handcuffed detainees and children.The Independent Inquiry relating to Afghanistan is examining allegations that the SAS murdered people during detention operations in Afghanistan between 2010 and 2013, and that senior officials sought to cover up the true circumstances of the killings.It is also examining whether the Royal Military Police's investigations into such killings were adequate.The RMP evidence is a rare glimpse into the public inquiry's work - much of the evidence is being heard in closed-door hearings.In January of last year, in the last public evidence sessions, the inquiry heard from its expert witness Alan Pughsley, former chief constable of Kent Police and experienced homicide investigator.He described how the incredibly complex investigation as fundamentally poorly resourced "from start to finish", hampered by "indecision and apathy" from senior officers, as well as a lack of cooperation from UK Special Forces command.Pughsley was clear he would not have closed the investigation, particularly at a time when major lines of inquiry were still outstanding.Do you have information about this story that you want to share?Get in touch using SecureDrop, a highly anonymous and secure way of whistleblowing to the BBC which uses the TOR network.Or by using the Signal messaging app, an end-to-end encrypted message service designed to protect your data.SecureDrop: http://kt2bqe753wj6dgarak2ryj4d6a5tccrivbvod5ab3uxhug5fi624vsqd.onion/Signal: 0044 7714 956 936Please note that the SecureDrop link will only work in a Tor browser. title: Why the Prime Minister wants to talk about Brexit again
description: The Brexit debate is back.For years, it felt like the only thing Westminster talked about.I have had a ringside seat at it all, from the Conservative
body: The Brexit debate is back.For years, it felt like the only thing Westminster talked about.I have had a ringside seat at it all, from the Conservative election victory in 2015, with the party's promise in its manifesto that year to offer "a straight in-out referendum on our membership of the European Union by the end of 2017."Then there was the then Prime Minister David Cameron's negotiation with the European Union to try to secure what he saw as a better deal and then the referendum itself on Thursday, 23 June 2016.And that, you will remember, was merely the start, as years of wrangling began. Two general elections came and went in 2017 and 2019 and it took the two prime ministers after David Cameron, first Theresa May and then Boris Johnson, before the UK left the European Union at 23:00 on Friday, 31 January 2020.Little wonder perhaps that by that point, almost irrespective of someone's views on the topic, there was an appetite to talk about something else. Anything else. Political parties picked up that vibe and while their long standing instincts on the EU were there to see if you scratched the surface, there was minimal desire to extemporise about them any time soon.With the arrival of Andy Burnham as prime minister, that has changed, despite what he said just a few months before he arrived in Downing Street. He has been happy to repeatedly lean into an argument claiming that it is time to "face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good" and "the status quo is not good enough for Britain." First he made this case at the Labour Party Conference last month and now he has made it again in the House of Commons.Burnham is attempting to make a two-pronged case. First, in the short term, he wants to "deepen" the UK's relationship with the EU at a summit in Brussels at the end of next month. He insists such a deepening would be within the promise made by Labour at the last general election that the UK would say no to the customs union, the single market and freedom of movement. Which brings us onto the second element of his case, in the medium term. What might Labour promise in its next general election manifesto? The prime minister told me a fortnight ago the manifesto could promise an in-out referendum.In the Commons, he sought to reassure you, whatever your view on Brexit. "This country in the next decade needs to know where it's going. There are no assumptions here, and as I said, the British public will be the boss of whatever is decided," he said.Hang on, say critics, it was decided by voters a decade ago. "They weighed the arguments and made a decision. The least they are owed is politicians willing to defend it," argues Lord Frost, external, a former Brexit minister and chief Brexit negotiator in the Telegraph.The focus of the next five weeks, ahead of a UK-EU Summit in Brussels on Friday 20 November, is what Downing Street sees as short term wins on youth mobility, food and drink, and energy.Andy Burnham hopes to make an argument that what he will portray as a sensible, pragmatic deepening of the relationship with Brussels can help cut illegal immigration and boost economic growth.He sought to goad the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch for seeking to oppose a plan he thinks can contribute to growth. She argued it risked regurgitating yesterday's arguments with little prospect of success.And, strikingly, his attempt at goading his opponents went further still. He told The Rest Is Politics podcast that upon arriving in Downing Street, he had asked if there was Russian interference in the Brexit referendum. "I've had a clear answer that, yes, there was," he claimed, without saying who provided that clear answer or what the evidence for that suggested clarity was.In the Commons, his language appeared a little softer. He told MPs it was "inconceivable" to think that Russia did not try to interfere.  A double negative deployed this time, about alleged attempts at interference.His political opponents were already pouncing. The Reform UK leader Nigel Farage was blunt – calling the prime minister "a liar."The former Prime Minister Boris Johnson added that he had asked the same question as Andy Burnham did when he became Foreign Secretary, external "and they replied that there was no evidence of any successful interference in the 2016 referendum, by Russia or any other power".And so a debate resumes about the difference between attempted interference, interference and successful interference.But the key point is this: for the first time since the UK left the European Union, we now have a prime minister who is willing to unflinchingly debate Brexit: whether it is working, how it is working, how to improve it, and if it's proved to be a failure.In so doing he hopes he can tap into public sentiment which opinion polls suggest a perception among a majority that leaving the European Union hasn't turned out how many might have hoped., externalOn top of this, he hopes to lure pro Europeans broadly on the Left who may recently have supported the Liberal Democrats, the Green parties of both England and Wales and Scotland, the Scottish National Party and Plaid Cymru towards Labour. That is the political logic from the government's point of view, for now at least.And as for where all of this leads – well, good question. In the coming weeks, months and perhaps years, there may be a Back to the Future vibe to our political debate. A splash of familiarity, as a conversation about the relationship we have with our nearest neighbours resumes.

schema.headline: Why the Prime Minister wants to talk about Brexit again
